profiles.authors: Geoff Pike and Jyrki Alakuijala · Google
profiles.background: CityHash is Google’s family of noncryptographic string hashes, drawing on earlier work by Austin Appleby and Bob Jenkins. CityHash64 was designed with short strings and hash-table keys in mind.

results.city: Two different eight-byte messages reach the same public hash before the seed is applied. The seeded wrapper therefore returns the same result for every seed.

profiles.background: FarmHash continues Google’s work on fast string hashing after CityHash. The library includes several implementations selected for different processors; the point here is specifically the NA variant’s seeded 64-bit function.

results.farm: Like CityHash’s seeded wrapper, this variant compresses the message before applying the secret. The eight-byte witness pair already agrees at that point, so changing the seed cannot separate it.

profiles.background: MurmurHash3 belongs to the same project as the original SMHasher test suite. Its name reflects its use of multiplication and rotation. The x64_128 variant maintains two 64-bit state words and returns 128 bits.

results.murmur: A controlled difference survives the public word mixing and is cancelled by later message words. The selected pair collides in the full 128-bit output for every 32-bit API seed.

profiles.background: mx3 grew out of work on bit mixers and supplies a mixer, a pseudorandom generator, and a string hash. Version 3 revised the hash’s seeding and speed while retaining its multiply-and-xorshift design.

results.mx3: A one-byte message and an eight-byte message cancel their public length and word terms. Both leave the same seed-dependent state, giving an every-seed collision.

profiles.background: fasthash is a compact C design built around multiplication and xorshift mixing. The project describes its mixing function as learned using genetic programming. It offers both 64-bit and 32-bit outputs.

results.fasthash-64: The selected seven-byte and eight-byte messages cancel the different length terms before the common finalizer. The same construction collides for every seed at both output widths.
results.fasthash-32: The selected seven-byte and eight-byte messages cancel the different length terms before the common finalizer. The same construction collides for every seed at both output widths.

profiles.background: MuseAir is a portable design using widening multiplication. The record here is the historical v0.3 implementation retained in SMHasher3; later upstream algorithm versions must be considered separately.

results.muse: A public zero-product operand makes a changed message word disappear before secret mixing. The fixed pair collides for every seed in the studied v0.3 implementation.

profiles.background: komihash is a header-only C/C++ hash from the author of a5hash. Its multiplication-based design keeps the high and low halves of products in separate state variables and processes long inputs through parallel lanes.

results.komi: Two messages differing in just two bits collide for about 91.06% of sampled seeds. Public relations between lanes allow the changes to cancel. This construction applies only to lengths 64–127 bytes.

profiles.background: t1ha (“Fast Positive Hash”) is a family of noncryptographic hashes with separate variants for different platforms and uses. This point is t1ha2’s one-shot 64-bit function, not its streaming or 128-bit API.

results.t1ha: The 16-byte and 11-byte witness messages exploit carry patterns for a structured class of seeds. The cap combines an exact class size with a measured success rate inside that class.

profiles.background: a5hash is a header-only C/C++ family aimed at hash tables and hash maps, from the author of komihash. It supplies 64-bit and 128-bit functions. Both plotted results concern v5.21.

results.a5: An exactly counted class of seeds makes a multiplication erase a message word. This proves a lower bound on one pair’s collision probability, and therefore an upper cap on the family’s score.
results.a5wide: A public zero-product operand erases a changed word for every seed. Both output words collide, despite this tested 128-bit variant passing all 250 published SMHasher3 tests.

profiles.authors: Nicolas De Carli · based on wyhash by Wang Yi
profiles.background: rapidhash builds on wyhash’s widening-multiplication approach. Its standard, Micro, and Nano variants trade throughput against code size. The plotted benchmark is the standard v3 implementation.

results.rapid3: Complementing both operands of an early multiplication can leave its high/low fold unchanged. The measured pair gives an upper cap, not a ranking against other hashes whose searches used different budgets.

profiles.background: MUM stands for “multiply and mix”: it combines the halves of a wide product to mix bits. The project also contains pseudorandom generators. This post studies the pre-fix v3 design with fixed public constants.

results.mum: Two distinct eight-byte words have the same public multiplication fold before they meet the seeded state. The every-seed result concerns pre-fix MUM v3, not the later collision-prevention default.

profiles.background: mir’s hash lives in the MIR compiler project and uses multiplication followed by addition of the high and low halves. It includes native-wide and decomposed-multiplication implementations; this chart uses mir.exact timings.

results.mir: Two eight-byte words yield the same zero public fold, leaving identical seeded states. The selected pair works in both the exact and inexact implementations.

profiles.authors: Yann Collet and the xxHash contributors
profiles.background: XXH3 extends the xxHash family with 64-bit and 128-bit outputs and optimized paths for different input lengths and CPUs. These results use v0.8.3’s seeded API with the default public secret.

results.xxh3-64: Complementing the first two words can preserve their multiplication fold. The measured cap comes from a selected fixed pair; it is not a demonstrated flooding attack or a result for independently randomized custom secrets.
results.xxh3-128: The selected pair preserves both an early product fold and the relevant word sum. Both halves of the 128-bit output are compared: the measured collisions are full-output collisions.

profiles.authors: Jyrki Alakuijala, Bill Cox, and Jan Wassenberg · Google
profiles.background: Introduced in a 2016 paper, HighwayHash uses SIMD multiplication and permutation with a 256-bit key. It was designed as a fast keyed hash and pseudorandom function, with 64-bit, 128-bit, and 256-bit outputs.

results.highway: A rare, explicitly counted key event lets a 96-byte pair merge the entire internal state before finalization. The cap uses that sufficient event; it is not an exact total collision probability.

profiles.background: SpookyHash is Jenkins’s noncryptographic 128-bit hash, designed for 64-bit machines, with wrappers for shorter outputs. The V2 revision corrected issues in the original design; this point is its 64-bit wrapper.

results.spooky: A late-injected difference cancels in the internal state before finalization. The selected pair collides for about half the sampled seeds; exact half balance has not been proved.

profiles.background: pengyhash is a compact noncryptographic 64-bit hash built from additions, rotations, and XORs. Version 0.3 uses a 64-bit seed, whereas earlier versions used 32 bits.

results.pengyhash: The bulk loop never uses the seed. Two messages reach the same public state before seeded finalization, so they collide for every seed. This record uses SMHasher3’s sequenced v0.3 implementation.

profiles.background: NMHASH32 and NMHASH32X are separate functions in the hash-garage project. Both return 32 bits and accept a 32-bit seed, but use different mixing designs. The two points retain their own witnesses and measurements.

results.nmhash32: A difference passes through a lane under specific seed-bit and carry conditions, then cancels in later words. Exhaustive enumeration counts the successful seeds; this is not the every-seed result of NMHASH32X.
results.nmhash32x: A controlled difference becomes a top-bit change through public mixing. Two later message words cancel both state differences for every seed.

profiles.background: gxhash is a Rust hash designed around hardware AES instructions. It uses parallel processing to obtain high throughput and provides several output widths. This point is the studied 64-bit v3.5.0 implementation.

results.gx: The selected 15-byte and 16-byte inputs collide in public compression before the seed can distinguish them. The resulting pair collides for every seed.

profiles.background: aHash is a Rust hash-table hasher that uses AES instructions when available, with a separate fallback design. This post’s result is specifically for the AES path in version 0.8.12.

results.ahash: A chosen difference cancels in both the AES and shuffled-addition accumulators. The measured result uses four independent internal key words in the validated C reproduction; transfer to native Rust depends on the operation and constructor mapping.

profiles.background: PolymurHash combines polynomial hashing over a prime field with a Murmur-inspired final mixer. It aims to provide a universal hash using ordinary widening multiplication, without requiring carry-less multiplication instructions.

results.polymur: The audit recovers a full-output guarantee using a rigorous lower bound on the allowed key set’s size. It requires a uniform key from that restricted set; the shipped seed distribution and stronger ASU claim remain uncertified.

profiles.background: HalftimeHash’s 2021 paper targets long strings without widening 64-bit multiplication or finite-field arithmetic. The four plotted styles are implementation variants: all return 64-bit hashes, despite the numbers in their names.

results.halftimehash-64: The wrapper proof gap is closed: the audited contract gives a score of at least 63 bits with independent entropy and finite, style-specific length caps. This certificate does not cover literal ISO-C++ portability, seed expansion, or the separate advanced API.
results.halftimehash-128: The wrapper proof gap is closed: the audited contract gives a score of at least 63 bits with independent entropy and finite, style-specific length caps. This certificate does not cover literal ISO-C++ portability, seed expansion, or the separate advanced API.
results.halftimehash-256: The wrapper proof gap is closed: the audited contract gives a score of at least 63 bits with independent entropy and finite, style-specific length caps. This certificate does not cover literal ISO-C++ portability, seed expansion, or the separate advanced API.
results.halftimehash-512: The wrapper proof gap is closed: the audited contract gives a score of at least 63 bits with independent entropy and finite, style-specific length caps. This certificate does not cover literal ISO-C++ portability, seed expansion, or the separate advanced API.

profiles.background: UMASH was introduced at Backtrace in 2020 to combine fast string hashing with collision bounds. It also computes a second hash alongside the first to produce a 128-bit fingerprint.

results.umash: The hollow point retains the published claim, whose projection argument has a gap. The current audit proves a weaker 25.6-bit fallback (also inherited by the fingerprint), and no collision violating the claimed production bound is known.
results.umash128: The hollow point retains the published claim, whose projection argument has a gap. The current audit proves a weaker 25.6-bit fallback (also inherited by the fingerprint), and no collision violating the claimed production bound is known.

profiles.background: CLHASH uses carry-less multiplication instructions to accelerate universal hashing. Its construction was published as “Faster 64-bit universal hashing using carry-less multiplications.”

results.clhash: The plotted guarantee is for ideal Algorithm 4 with its full independent key. The timed implementation’s seed initializer is not certified by that theorem.

profiles.authors: Thomas Dybdahl Ahle · author of this post
profiles.background: ChainHash is the author’s construction in the fast-polynomials project. This point uses 256-byte blocks and the model A key distribution, which takes 80 independent random key bytes.

results.chain256: The current model A theorem gives a 61-bit lower score guarantee. Its structured polynomial keys differ from the 41-independent-word reference theorem checked in Lean. The timed SplitMix64 initializer and compiler/SIMD correctness have separate status.

profiles.background: Poly1305 is the polynomial-hashing component of Bernstein’s Poly1305-AES authenticator. It works modulo 2¹³⁰ − 5 with a restricted (“clamped”) polynomial key and produces a 128-bit tag.

results.poly1305: The 103-bit score comes from the published collision bound, which was not re-audited here. The benchmark includes the OpenSSL 3 wrapper and seed setup; the theorem requires its stated uniform key distribution.

profiles.authors: David A. McGrew and John Viega · GCM construction
profiles.background: GHASH is the universal-hashing component of Galois/Counter Mode (GCM). It evaluates a polynomial over the binary field GF(2¹²⁸); GCM combines that hash with counter-mode encryption.

results.ghash: The 127-bit score comes from the published bound under a uniform field key, not a new audit. Throughput is an OpenSSL GMAC proxy including wrapper and setup costs, not a bare GHASH benchmark.
